stories.headline: Update: FISA Spy Powers Near Lapse as Trump Refuses to Drop Pulte Nomination
stories.summary:
A lapse in Section 702 of the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act grew more likely Wednesday as President Trump resisted bipartisan pressure to replace acting Director of National Intelligence Bill Pulte, whose appointment Democrats have made a condition for renewing the surveillance law. The law, which allows the U.S. to collect intelligence on foreign targets abroad, expires at midnight Friday — a deadline that coincides with the opening of World Cup games in American cities and approaching celebrations for the nation's 250th anniversary.

Trump asked Congress for a short-term extension to allow time to nominate a permanent DNI, but refused to withdraw Pulte's acting appointment, saying he would not let Democrats 'extort' the administration. Senate Republicans floated a stopgap extension, which Democrats immediately rejected. Speaker Mike Johnson announced a House vote Thursday on a measure to extend the program through July 2, though passage appeared uncertain.

Democrats, led by House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, argue Pulte is a 'partisan political hack' unqualified for the intelligence post and that Trump must name a permanent replacement before they will vote for any extension. Senate Majority Leader John Thune said Republican leadership has communicated to the White House what is needed to pass the bill. Trump said he is interviewing five candidates for the permanent role, all with national security backgrounds.

The standoff represents a rare instance of intelligence-community tools being used as a political bargaining chip, with national security implications if the program lapses even briefly. Critics on both sides of the aisle have warned that allowing Section 702 authorities to go dark — even temporarily — could blind U.S. intelligence to foreign threats at a sensitive moment.

stories.headline: Update: Vance Says Netanyahu 'Has Got Some Things Wrong' as U.S.-Israel Tensions Surface
stories.summary:
Vice President JD Vance said in an interview set to air Sunday that Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has 'certainly gotten some things wrong,' offering the most direct public acknowledgment yet of friction between the two allies. Vance told CBS News that Netanyahu 'aggressively asserts the interests of his country,' but that those interests are not always aligned with those of the United States, and that when they diverge, the Trump administration must 'choose the side of the American people.'

The remarks come as the U.S. and Iran exchanged strikes for a second consecutive day, straining a ceasefire in place since April. The renewed hostilities were triggered in part by Israel's continued military operation in Lebanon against Hezbollah, which Tehran has demanded be addressed in any broader peace agreement. Israel has argued Lebanon was not part of the April ceasefire framework.

Trump last week was reported to have called Netanyahu 'effing crazy' in a phone call over the Lebanon operations, saying he was 'perturbed' by Israel's continued fighting there. Vance declined to specify where he believed Netanyahu had erred, saying 'those conversations are sometimes better left in private.' The comments mark a notable public distancing from a leader Trump has historically championed.

The diplomatic strain has significant implications for U.S. efforts to broker a wider ceasefire with Iran, which has made Israel's Lebanon campaign a sticking point in negotiations. Supporters of the U.S.-Israel alliance argue Washington should back Israel's right to defend itself; critics say unchecked Israeli operations risk widening a conflict the administration has sought to contain.

stories.headline: Feds Will Not Seek Death Penalty in Plea Deal for Suspect in Political Assassination of Minnesota Lawmaker
stories.summary:
Federal prosecutors announced Wednesday they will not seek the death penalty against Vance Boelter, the man charged with the political assassinations of former Minnesota House Speaker Melissa Hortman and her husband, as part of a plea agreement. Boelter was scheduled for a change-of-plea hearing Thursday in federal court in Minneapolis. The court filing did not detail the full terms of the agreement.

Boelter, 58, is accused of shooting the Hortmans and seriously wounding state Sen. John Hoffman and his wife Yvette in the early hours of June 14, 2025. Prosecutors say he came to their doors disguised as a police officer driving a fake squad car. He was captured the following day after what authorities called the largest manhunt in Minnesota history, and faces both federal and state charges.

Minnesota abolished the death penalty in 1911 and has no history of federal capital cases, raising legal questions about whether the case met the federal threshold for capital punishment. The Trump administration has broadly pushed for expanded use of the death penalty. Prosecutors had previously called the attacks politically motivated, releasing a handwritten letter in which Boelter allegedly confessed, though his precise motive remained unclear.

Sen. Hoffman, who survived the attack, said in a lawsuit filed in April that his left arm and hand would likely never fully recover and that he sustained permanent internal injuries. Boelter's state case has been held in abeyance pending resolution of federal charges.

stories.headline: RSF Drone Strike on Funeral Procession Kills at Least 4 in Sudan's El-Obeid
stories.summary:
A drone strike struck a funeral procession at a cemetery in the Sudanese city of el-Obeid on Wednesday, killing at least four people and wounding several others, according to two rights groups, Sudan Doctors Network and Emergency Lawyers. Both organizations attributed the attack to the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces. Emergency Lawyers said the cemetery strike was part of a broader series of drone attacks that evening in which at least 23 people died in total, including strikes on homes, the airport district, and areas near an army base.

El-Obeid is currently under army control and has become a major front line in Sudan's three-year civil war, which began after the leaders of the army and the RSF broke over the country's political future. The city sits in the oil-rich Kordofan region, and analysts say control of the area effectively determines control of Sudan's oil supply as well as a key geographic corridor between RSF-dominated western territory and army-held eastern regions.

The ongoing conflict has produced what the United Nations has called the world's worst humanitarian crisis, with more than 11 million people displaced and 28 million facing acute hunger. The confirmed death toll is at least 50,000, though reliable figures are difficult to obtain. Residents described scenes of collapsed houses with no survivors visible.

The attacks on civilian gatherings, including a funeral and a food-supply convoy, drew condemnation from rights groups who described them as systematic and repeated targeting of non-combatants in el-Obeid over several days.

stories.headline: Update: Israeli Strikes Kill 17 in Southern Lebanon as U.S.-Iran Ceasefire Frays
stories.summary:
Israeli air and artillery strikes killed at least 17 people in southern Lebanon on Wednesday, according to Lebanon's state-run National News Agency. Nine died in the town of Tayr Debba alone, with additional casualties in Deir Qanoun el-Nahr, Seddiqin, and Sidon. The Israeli military did not immediately comment on Wednesday's strikes but confirmed it had targeted Hezbollah infrastructure and rocket launchers in the area on Tuesday.

Hezbollah announced retaliatory rocket and shell attacks on Israeli troop positions in southern Lebanon. The escalation comes as Iran demands that any ceasefire deal with the U.S. and Israel also cover Lebanon — a condition Israel has rejected, arguing Lebanon was not part of the April ceasefire agreement. The UN human rights chief announced he is dispatching investigators to Lebanon to examine possible violations by all parties since March.

The fighting deepens a diplomatic crisis for the Trump administration, which has been pressing for a broader peace deal. U.S. Vice President JD Vance, in an interview set to air Sunday, said Israeli Prime Minister Netanyahu has "gotten some things wrong" and that U.S. and Israeli interests are not always aligned. Trump himself has reportedly clashed with Netanyahu over the Lebanon campaign, and last week was quoted calling him "effing crazy" over the continued fighting.

The Lebanon front is now a central obstacle to ending the wider Iran-Israel-U.S. conflict. Tehran has threatened to suspend peace talks unless Lebanon is covered, while Israel maintains its Hezbollah campaign is a separate security imperative. The UN probe adds further pressure, with evidence potentially usable in war crimes prosecutions.

stories.headline: UK Defence Secretary John Healey Resigns, Deepening Starmer's Political Crisis
stories.summary:
UK Defence Secretary John Healey resigned from Prime Minister Keir Starmer's cabinet on Thursday, culminating a months-long dispute with the Treasury over military spending levels. Healey cited constraints placed on his long-delayed defence investment plan by Chancellor of the Exchequer Rachel Reeves. The resignation comes at a moment of heightened pressure on Starmer, with rivals reportedly lining up to challenge for the Labour leadership.

Business Secretary Peter Kyle acknowledged the resignation publicly but said he did not know the full circumstances, telling Bloomberg he believed the government was "investing enormously" in defence. Healey's departure marks a significant blow to Starmer's authority on a portfolio — military readiness and NATO commitments — that has been central to Labour's governing agenda amid the ongoing conflicts in the Middle East and Eastern Europe.

The resignation echoes broader tensions within European NATO allies over defence budgets, coming weeks after Germany cancelled its joint fighter programme with France. Britain has faced mounting pressure from Washington and from within the alliance to increase defence spending toward and beyond the NATO target of 2 percent of GDP. Healey had publicly advocated for faster and deeper investment.

Starmer now faces the politically sensitive task of appointing a new defence secretary while managing a fractious parliamentary party and a country increasingly concerned about security spending. The resignation is likely to intensify internal Labour debate over the government's economic priorities.

stories.headline: Belfast Riots Enter Third Night After Sudanese Man Charged With Attempted Murder in Stabbing
stories.summary:
Police in Northern Ireland deployed water cannons for a second night Wednesday as protesters set fires and hurled bricks, rocks and bottles in Belfast and Newtownabbey. The unrest followed a brutal stabbing attack that left a man seriously injured and blinded in one eye. A 30-year-old Sudanese national, Hadi Alodid, appeared before Belfast Magistrates' Court charged with attempted murder, possession of a knife, and threatening to kill a hospital radiographer during treatment for injuries he sustained.

A detective told the court that police found Alodid on top of the victim armed with a kitchen knife. At the hospital, Alodid reportedly told staff "I've killed someone, I don't know if they are dead" and threatened to kill a radiographer. He refused legal representation through an Arabic interpreter and did not enter a plea. He was ordered held in custody.

The violence has taken on an anti-immigrant character: masked rioters on Tuesday set fire to homes they believed to house immigrants and burned vehicles. Demonstrators used sledgehammers to break up pavements and dismantled fences for use as shields against police. Police were bracing for further disorder as the court proceedings drew additional public attention to the case.

The riots represent a serious public order crisis for Northern Ireland authorities and raise broader questions about immigration-related tensions in the UK. Community and political leaders have called for calm, while rights groups have urged the public not to conflate the actions of an individual with immigrant communities as a whole.

stories.headline: NOAA Declares El Niño Under Way, Warns of Potentially Record-Breaking Event by Late 2026
stories.summary:
The U.S. National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration officially declared an El Niño event under way on Thursday, with sea surface temperatures in the central and eastern tropical Pacific having crossed the 0.5 degrees Celsius above-average threshold used to define the phenomenon. Scientists said the atmospheric response — a shift in equatorial Pacific winds — confirms the warming is now a full El Niño, not merely an oceanic anomaly.

NOAA said its models give a 63 percent probability that the event will reach "very strong" intensity — above 2 degrees Celsius above average — during the November-through-January peak period, potentially ranking it among the three or four largest El Niño events since records began in 1950. Some U.S. and European models show Pacific sea surface temperatures potentially rising more than 3 degrees Celsius above average by year's end, though NOAA urged caution in interpreting those projections.

The concern among scientists is that this El Niño is developing on top of a planet already substantially warmer than historical baselines due to long-term climate change. A typical strong El Niño adds roughly 0.2 degrees Celsius to global average air temperatures; experts warn the actual regional impacts this time could be unprecedented given the elevated starting point. Effects typically include severe drought in parts of Africa and Asia, heavy rainfall and flooding in the Americas, and disruptions to agriculture and food supply chains worldwide.

A very strong El Niño could make 2027 the hottest year on record globally, scientists said, with economic and humanitarian consequences extending well into that year. The last three comparable events — in 1982-83, 1997-98, and 2015-16 — each caused widespread damage to crops, infrastructure, and public health across multiple continents.

stories.headline: Update: Iran Strikes U.S. Bases in Kuwait, Jordan, and Bahrain as Conflict Widens; IAEA Demands Nuclear Access
stories.summary:
The United States and Iran exchanged strikes for a second consecutive day, with Tehran claiming it targeted American military assets in Kuwait, Jordan, and Bahrain overnight, with Bahrain reporting damage to its capital. The renewed hostilities followed U.S. airstrikes against Iranian defense systems and came after President Trump accused Iran of taking "too long to make a deal," though the immediate trigger was Israel's continued campaign against Hezbollah in Lebanon. Three Indian sailors missing after a U.S. strike on a sanctioned tanker in the Gulf of Oman have been confirmed dead by the Indian government.

Iran is also demanding that any ceasefire agreement with the U.S. and Israel formally cover Lebanon, a condition Israel has rejected, deepening the diplomatic impasse. Israel conducted fresh strikes in southern Lebanon killing at least 17 people, and BBC Verify analysis indicates Iran has damaged 20 U.S. military sites since the conflict's start. U.N. human rights chief Volker Türk announced he is sending investigators to Lebanon to examine potential war crimes by all parties.

Separately, the IAEA's board of governors voted 21-to-3 on Wednesday to demand Iran fully cooperate with nuclear inspectors, provide complete information about its stockpile of near-weapons-grade uranium, and grant access to nuclear sites struck during the June 2025 war. Russia, China, and Niger opposed the resolution. The IAEA director-general has warned Iran's existing stockpile of 440.9 kilograms of uranium enriched to 60% purity is sufficient material — if further enriched — for as many as 10 nuclear bombs. Iran denies pursuing nuclear weapons.

Vice President JD Vance, in a CBS News interview due to air Sunday, said Israeli Prime Minister Netanyahu "has gotten some things wrong" and that U.S. and Israeli interests are not always aligned, marking one of the most public admissions of strain between the two allies. Trump reportedly called Netanyahu "effing crazy" last week over Lebanon operations. Analysts say Iran appears emboldened by the conflict's trajectory, sensing the White House has limited appetite for escalation, while the U.S. continues to push for a negotiated deal.

stories.headline: Thailand Sentences Two Uyghur Men to Death for 2015 Bangkok Shrine Bombing That Killed 20
stories.summary:
A Thai court has found two men guilty of carrying out the 2015 bombing of the Erawan Shrine in central Bangkok and sentenced them to death, concluding a ten-year trial for the country's deadliest terrorist attack. The blast killed 20 people and injured more than 120 at the popular tourist site on August 17, 2015. Both men, Bilal Mohammad and Yusufu Mierali, are from China's Uyghur minority and pleaded not guilty throughout proceedings.

The verdict has been clouded by significant questions about the integrity of the investigation. Key security cameras at the scene were found to be non-functional, and Thai authorities ordered the blast site cleaned and reopened within two days, hampering evidence collection. Police initially said neither arrested man matched the suspect seen on video planting a backpack at the shrine, and arrest warrants for 13 other suspects were never resolved, with many having already fled Thailand.

The case has long been linked to Thailand's controversial July 2015 decision to forcibly repatriate 109 Uyghur men to China, which prompted widespread international condemnation. Critics and human rights observers have argued the investigation was conducted under political pressure and that flaws in the process leave serious doubts over whether the convicted men were the true perpetrators. The Thai government has not publicly addressed the gaps in the case.

stories.headline: Pope Leo XIV Visits Canary Islands to Spotlight Migrant Deaths in Atlantic Crossing
stories.summary:
Pope Leo XIV began a visit to Spain's Canary Islands on Thursday, using the trip to draw attention to migrants who die attempting the Atlantic crossing from West Africa to Europe's southernmost territory. The Pope is expected to drop flowers into the ocean in memory of those who perished, including entire boatloads that vanished without trace, and to call for "safe and legal pathways" to Europe alongside a "respectful welcome" for those who arrive.

The visit comes as European political debate over migration has intensified. Spanish government data indicate sea arrivals to Spain have fallen this year partly due to increased EU-funded naval interceptions off the West African coast, but aid workers and clergy on the ground say deaths remain common. The Pope's emphasis on humanitarian reception stands in deliberate contrast to the rhetoric of migration as an "ideological invasion" prevalent in several European political movements.

The Canary Islands have become a focal point for Atlantic migration routes, with tens of thousands of people from sub-Saharan Africa attempting the crossing annually in search of entry to Europe. Local organizations working with migrants, including the Good Samaritan Foundation run by a Tenerife parish priest, argue the labor market could absorb many arrivals but that legal integration pathways remain severely limited. The Pope's visit is his first major foreign trip focused exclusively on migration policy.

stories.headline: Extreme Rain Event Killed 7 Percent of World's Rarest Orangutans, Study Finds
stories.summary:
A new study published Wednesday finds that four days of catastrophic rainfall from Cyclone Senyar in November 2025 killed at least 58 Tapanuli orangutans on the Indonesian island of Sumatra — roughly 7 percent of the entire species, which numbers fewer than 800 individuals. The figures are described as conservative and do not account for additional deaths from canopy damage or reduced food availability following the storm. The species was only formally identified in 2017 and is considered critically endangered.

Cyclone Senyar was Southeast Asia's deadliest natural disaster of 2025, killing more than 1,000 people across the region. Researchers say human-induced climate change played a significant role in the storm's severity and warn that the frequency and intensity of extreme rainfall events in the Tapanuli range is likely to increase. Studies indicate the species will face extinction if it loses more than 1 percent of its population annually — a threshold this single event exceeded more than sevenfold.

The Indonesian government has temporarily halted major development projects in the Batang Toru forest area of Sumatra, including mining, palm oil expansion, and hydropower construction, giving conservationists a rare window to assess and potentially stabilize the surviving population. Researchers say the findings underscore the compounding threat posed by extreme weather to already critically fragile wildlife populations and call for urgent policy action to protect remaining habitat.
